passages.original: Pythagoram, qui primum se esse philosophum nuncuparit, eum sui saeculi excellentissima forma fuisse; item Zenonem illum antiquum Velia oriundum, qui primus omnium ἀπορίας sollertissimo artificio ambifariam dissoluerit, eum quoque Zenonem longe decorissimum fuisse, ut Plato autumat; itemque multos philosophos ab ore honestissimos memoriae prodi, qui gratiam corporis morum honestamentis ornauerint. sed haec defensio, ut dixi, aliquam multum a me remota est, cui praeter formae mediocritatem continuatio etiam litterati laboris omnem gratiam corpore deterget, habitudinem tenuat, sucum exsorbet, colorem obliterat, uigorem debilitat.
passages.english: [I would have said] that Pythagoras, who was the first to call himself a philosopher, was of the most outstanding beauty of his age; likewise that the famous ancient Zeno, a native of Velia, who first of all men resolved *aporiai* [logical puzzles] by a most ingenious device on both sides, that this Zeno too was by far the most handsome, as Plato asserts; and likewise that many philosophers are recorded as most comely in face, who adorned the grace of the body with the beauties of character. But this defence, as I said, is very far removed from me, since, besides my middling looks, the unbroken continuance of literary labour also scours all grace from my body, thins my physique, drains my vigour, effaces my colour, and weakens my strength.
passages.notes: The opening infinitive clauses continue reported speech ('praeterea: licere...') from the preceding context; '[I would have said]' supplied. 'sucum' rendered 'vigour' (lit. 'sap, juice').

passages.original: De eloquentia uero, si qua mihi fuisset, neque mirum neque inuidiosum deberet uideri, si ab ineunte aeuo unis studiis litterarum ex summis uiribus deditus omnibus aliis spretis uoluptatibus ad hoc aeui haud sciam anne super omnis homines impenso labore diuque noctuque cum despectu et dispendio bonae valetudinis eam quaesissem. sed nihil ab eloquentia metuant, quam ego, si quid omnino promoui, potius spero quam praesto. sane quidem, si uerum est quod Statium Caecilium in suis poematibus scripsisse dicunt, innocentiam eloquentiam esse, ego uero profiteor ista ratione ac praefero me nemini omnium de eloquentia concessurum. quis enim me hoc quidem pacto eloquentior uiuat, quippe qui nihil unquam cogitaui quod eloqui non auderem?
passages.english: As for eloquence, if I had had any, it ought to seem neither surprising nor a cause for envy if, devoted from earliest youth with all my strength to the study of letters alone, scorning all other pleasures, I had sought it up to this time of life with labour expended, I would hardly know whether beyond all men, day and night, with contempt for and loss of good health. But let them fear nothing from eloquence, which I, if I have advanced at all, rather hope for than display. Certainly, if what they say Statius Caecilius wrote in his poems is true, that innocence is eloquence, then I indeed declare on that reckoning, and proclaim, that I will yield to no one at all in eloquence. For who living could be more eloquent than I on these terms, since I have never thought anything that I would not dare to speak out?

passages.original: quaeso, quid habent isti uersus re aut uerbo pudendum, quid omnino quod philosophus suum nolit uideri? nisi forte in eo reprehendendus sum, quod Calpurniano puluisculum ex Arabicis frugibus miserim, quem multo aequius erat spurcissimo ritu Hiberorum, ut ait Catullus, sua sibi urina dentem atque russam pumicare gingiuam.
passages.english: I ask you, what do these verses have that is shameful in matter or word, what at all that a philosopher would not wish to be seen as his own? Unless perhaps I am to be blamed in this, that I sent Calpurnianus a fine powder made from Arabian produce, when it was much more fitting for him, by the filthiest custom of the Iberians, as Catullus says, to scour his tooth and red gum with his own urine.

passages.original: hic illud etiam reprehendi animaduertisti, quod, cum aliis nominibus pueri uocentur, ego eos Charinum et Critian appellitarim. eadem igitur opera accusent C. Catullum, quod Lesbiam pro Clodia nominarit, et Ticidam similiter, quod quae Metella erat Perillam scripserit, et Propertium, qui Cunthiam dicat, Hostiam dissimulet, et Tibullum, quod ei sit Plania in animo, Delia in uersu. etquidem C. Lucilium, quanquam sit iambicus, tamen improbarim, quod Gentium et Macedonem pueros directis nominibus carmine suo prostituerit. quanto modestius tandem Mantuanus poeta, qui itidem ut ego puerum amici sui Pollionis bucolico ludicro laudans et abstinens nominum sese quidem Corydonem, puerum uero Alexin uocat.
passages.english: Here you noticed that this too was criticised: that, although the boys are called by other names, I have called them Charinus and Critias. By the same token, then, let them accuse Gaius Catullus, because he named Lesbia in place of Clodia, and Ticidas likewise, because he wrote 'Perilla' for the woman who was Metella, and Propertius, who says 'Cynthia' and conceals Hostia, and Tibullus, because Plania was in his mind, Delia in his verse. Indeed, I would even disapprove of Gaius Lucilius, although he is an iambic poet, because he exposed the boys Gentius and Macedo under their real names in his poem. How much more modest, after all, is the Mantuan poet, who, just like me, praising the boy of his friend Pollio in a pastoral entertainment and abstaining from names, calls himself Corydon and the boy Alexis.

passages.original: utrum igitur putas maiorem curam decoris in adseueranda oratione suscipiendam rhetori iurganti an philosopho obiurganti, apud iudices sorte ductos paulisper disceptanti an apud omnis homines semper disserenti, de finibus agrorum litiganti an de finibus bonorum et malorum docenti? quid, quod nec ob haec debet tantummodo philosophus speculum inuisere; nam saepe oportet non modo similitudinem suam, uerum etiam ipsius similitudinis rationem considerare: num, ut ait Epicurus, profectae a nobis imagines uelut quaedam exuuiae iugi fluore a corporibus manantes, cum leue aliquid et solidum offenderunt, illisae reflectantur et retro expressae contrauersim respondeant an, ut alii philosophi disputant, radii nostri seu mediis oculis proliquati et lumini extrario mixti atque ita uniti, ut Plato arbitratur, seu tantum oculis profecti sine ullo foris amminiculo, ut Archytas putat, seu intentu ae+ris facti, ut Stoici rentur, cum alicui corpori inciderunt spisso et splendido et leui, paribus angulis quibus inciderant resultent ad faciem suam reduces atque ita, quod extra tangant ac uisant, id intra speculum imaginentur.
passages.english: Which, then, do you think must take greater care for propriety in delivering speech: the rhetorician wrangling, or the philosopher rebuking; the one disputing briefly before judges drawn by lot, or the one discoursing always before all mankind; the one litigating about the boundaries of fields, or the one teaching about the ends of good and evil? What of the fact that a philosopher ought to look into a mirror not for these reasons only? For he must often consider not only his own likeness but also the cause of the likeness itself: whether, as Epicurus says, images proceeding from us, like a kind of sloughed skins flowing from bodies in a continuous stream, when they strike something smooth and solid, are dashed back and reflected, and, pressed out backwards, answer in reverse; or whether, as other philosophers argue, our rays, either streaming out from the middle of the eyes and mixed with external light and thus united, as Plato holds, or proceeding from the eyes alone without any outside aid, as Archytas thinks, or produced by tension of the air, as the Stoics believe, when they fall upon some dense, bright and smooth body, rebound at angles equal to those at which they fell, returning to one's own face, and thus represent within the mirror what they touch and see outside.

passages.original: an remedia nosse et ea conquirere magi potius esse quam medici, quam denique philosophi putas, qui illis non ad quaestum, sed ad suppetias usurust? ueteres quidem medici etiam carmina remedia uulnerum norant, ut omnis uetustatis certissimus auctor Homerus docet, qui facit Vlixi de uulnere sanguinem profluentem sisti cantamine. nihil enim, quod salutis ferendae gratia fit, criminosum est. at enim inquit piscem cui rei nisi malae proscidisti, quem tibi Themiscon seruus attulit?
passages.english: Or do you think that knowing remedies and seeking them out belongs to a magician rather than to a physician, or indeed to a philosopher, who will use them not for gain but for help? The ancient physicians even knew incantations as remedies for wounds, as Homer, the surest authority of all antiquity, teaches, who makes the blood flowing from Ulysses' wound be stanched by a chant. For nothing done for the sake of bringing health is criminal. 'But,' he says, 'for what purpose but an evil one did you cut open the fish that the slave Themison brought you?'

passages.original: quod ego gratulor nescire istos legisse me Theophrasti quoque περὶ δακέτων καὶ βλητ ῶν et Nicandri θηριακά; ceterum me etiam ueneficii reum postularent; at quidem hoc negotium ex lectione et aemulatione Aristoteli nactus sum, nonnihil et Platone meo adhortante, qui ait eum, qui ista uestiget, ἀμεταμέλητον παιδιὰν ἐν βίῳ παίζειν.
passages.english: I am glad these people do not know that I have also read Theophrastus' 'On Biting and Stinging Creatures' and Nicander's 'Theriaca'; otherwise they would also charge me with poisoning. But in fact I took up this pursuit from reading and emulating Aristotle, with some encouragement too from my Plato, who says that one who investigates such things 'plays a game in life that brings no regret'.

passages.original: fors fuat an ne sic quidem credat Aemilianus sola trecenta milia nummum scripta eorumque repetitionem filiis Pudentillae pacto datam. cape sis ipse tu manibus tuis tabulas istas, da impulsori tuo Rufino: legat, pudeat illum tumidi animi sui et ambitiosae mendicitatis; quippe ipse egens, nudus CCCC milibus nummum a creditore acceptis filiam dotauit, Pudentilla locuples femina trecentis milibus dotis fuit contenta et maritum habet, et multis saepe et ingentibus dotibus spretis, inani nomine tantulae dotis contentum, ceterum praeter uxorem suam nihil computantem, omnem supellectilem cunctasque diuitias in concordia coniugii et mutuo amore ponentem.
passages.english: Perhaps Aemilianus will not believe even so that only three hundred thousand sesterces were written down, and that their repayment was granted by the contract to Pudentilla's sons. Take those tablets yourself in your own hands, give them to your instigator Rufinus: let him read, let him be ashamed of his swollen pride and his ambitious beggary; for he himself, needy and destitute, dowered his daughter with four hundred thousand sesterces received from a creditor, while Pudentilla, a wealthy woman, was content with a dowry of three hundred thousand, and she has a husband who, though he has often spurned many huge dowries, is content with the empty name of so small a dowry, and who otherwise counts nothing besides his wife, placing all his household goods and all his riches in the harmony of marriage and mutual love.

passages.original: uenerat ad nos, priusquam istam donationem perficeret, cum dissimili isto fratre suo Pontianus, pedes nostros aduolutus ueniam et obliuionem praeteritorum omnium postularat, flens et manus nostras osculabundus ac dicens paenitere quod Rufino et similibus auscultarit. petit postea suppliciter, uti se Lolliano quoque Auito C. V. purgem, cui haud pridem tirocinio orationis suae fuerat a me commendatus; quippe compererat ante paucos dies omnia me, ut acta erant, ad eum perscripsisse.
passages.english: Before she completed that donation, Pontianus had come to us with that unlike brother of his, thrown himself at our feet, and begged pardon and forgetfulness of all that had passed, weeping and kissing our hands and saying he regretted having listened to Rufinus and men like him. Afterwards he asks humbly that I clear him also with Lollianus Avitus, *vir clarissimus* [a man of senatorial rank], to whom not long before he had been recommended by me at the start of his career as a speaker; for he had learned that a few days earlier I had written to him a full account of everything as it had happened.

passages.original: quamcumque orationem struxerit Auitus, ita illa erit undique sui perfecte absoluta, ut in illa neque Cato grauitatem requirat neque Laelius lenitatem nec Gracchus impetum nec Caesar calorem nec Hortensius distributionem nec Caluus argutias nec parsimoniam Salustius nec opulentiam Cicero: prorsus, inquam, ne omnis persequar, si Auitum audias, neque additum quicquam uelis neque detractum neque autem aliquid commutatum.
passages.english: Whatever speech Avitus has composed, it will be so completely finished on every side that in it Cato would not miss gravity, nor Laelius mildness, nor Gracchus force, nor Caesar warmth, nor Hortensius arrangement, nor Calvus subtlety, nor Sallust economy, nor Cicero richness. In short, I say, not to go through them all, if you hear Avitus you would wish nothing added, nothing taken away, and nothing altered either.

passages.original: ceterum ad haec, quae obiecistis, numera an binis uerbis respondeam. dentes splendidas: ignosce munditiis. specula inspicis: debet philosophus. uersus facis: licet fieri. pisces exploras: Aristoteles docet. lignum consecras: Plato suadet. uxorem ducis: leges iubent. prior natu ista est: solet fieri. lucrum sectatus es: dotalis accipe, donationem recordare, testamentum lege. quae si omnia affatim retudi, si calumnias omnes refutaui, si me in omnibus non modo criminibus, uerum etiam maledictis procul a culpa philosophiae tutus sum, si philosophiae honorem, qui mihi salute mea antiquior est, nusquam minui, immo contra ubique si cum septem pennis eum tenui: si haec, ut dico, ita sunt, possum securus existimationem tuam reuereri quam potestatem uereri, quod minus graue et uerendum mihi arbitror ac procons(ule) damnari quam si a tam bono tamque emendato uiro improber.
passages.english: But to these charges you have brought, count whether I answer in two words each. 'You polish your teeth': pardon cleanliness. 'You look into mirrors': a philosopher should. 'You write verses': it is permitted. 'You examine fish': Aristotle teaches it. 'You consecrate wood': Plato advises it. 'You marry a wife': the laws command it. 'She is older than you': it often happens. 'You pursued gain': take the dowry deed, recall the donation, read the will. If I have amply beaten back all these, if I have refuted all the slanders, if in all things, not only the charges but also the insults, I am safe and far from any fault against philosophy, if I have nowhere diminished the honour of philosophy, which is dearer to me than my own safety, but on the contrary everywhere have held it with seven feathers: if, as I say, these things are so, I can without anxiety respect your judgement rather than fear your power, since I consider it less grave and to be dreaded to be condemned by a proconsul than to be disapproved of by so good and so upright a man.
passages.notes: 'cum septem pennis' is obscure and probably corrupt; rendered literally. 'splendidas' read as 'splendidas [dentes]'/'splendidus'.
